source.title: MicroEdit: Neuron-level Knowledge Disentanglement and Localization in Lifelong Model Editing
source.authors: Shiqi Wang; Qi Wang; Run-Liang Niu; He Kong; Yi Chang

page_placements.theme: Units selected for one task or concept also serve others; ablation or editing has off-target effects

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures overlap in neuron activations across semantically unrelated language-model knowledge statements using a different method from the original vision examples.
record.gate_note: Figure 1(e–f) and its accompanying text report activation overlap across knowledge statements. The paper also reports neuron activation rates, masking results, and editing performance, but those results do not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The Top-k and ablation results concern editing performance, not the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.
record.test_reason: An editing-method paper that cites polysemanticity (Bricken 2023, Elhage 2022) as motivation and reports mainly editing performance. Its only related analysis, Figure 1(e–f), counts shared activated neurons between pairs of knowledge statements (up to 18% overlap) for one unnamed model and layer. That pairwise overlap measures something related but different. It does not show that individual MLP neurons encode unrelated features, gives no share of polysemantic neurons, and has no baseline for chance overlap. So it does not test V2 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors assume neuron polysemanticity causes Knowledge Entanglement in editing. They report activation overlap as illustration and propose MicroEdit, which uses a pretrained overcomplete Top-k SAE to encourage monosemantic representations. They report that it outperforms baselines in lifelong editing on LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-7B. They also attribute degradation at 10K edits to near-unavoidable neuron polysemy, without testing this.
record.recipe_differences: Measures activation similarities across language-model knowledge statements rather than using the original vision-neuron examples; no direct replication of the original measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis uses both all-token averages and last-token activations, but the text does not report a method-specific difference in the outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: In one LLM, semantically unrelated knowledge statements (e.g. bananas/potassium vs geocentric Sun) share up to 18% of activated neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unrelated factual inputs share a measurable fraction of activated neurons in LLMs, causing interference when editing (knowledge entanglement).

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: For the activation-overlap analysis, the text does not identify the model or report its size, does not quantify the share of neurons with mixed responses, and gives no uncertainty estimate or control. The reported up-to-18% overlap is not assigned to either token-aggregation condition in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1(a–c) activation-rate and masking results, and Tables 1–6 and related editing ablations, were left out because they report activation sparsity or editing performance rather than whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Figure 1(d) semantic-similarity results describe the statements, not neuron responses.

untested.parts: No share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no layer comparison of polysemanticity.
Superposition as the cause is cited, not tested.
No comparison across architectures or activation functions. The SAE is an add-on decoder, not a change to the model's own neurons.
Two token aggregations are shown, but no comparison of polysemanticity classification across them.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V2 limits_scope label is removed, because the overlap analysis is a motivating illustration of a different construct, not a test. The Top-k result (larger k means more neuron sharing and interference) concerns SAE latents and editing performance, not model neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish the share of all MLP neurons that respond to unrelated contexts, does not report an MLP-specific analysis, and does not measure responses to unrelated tokens.
No test of whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
No test of polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise in networks with sufficient neurons.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across activation functions or architectures, and no measurement showing that such a share can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
No investigation of whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.

The paper computes activation similarities using all-token averages and last-token activations, but does not report a result establishing that the polysemanticity finding changes with the measurement choice.

relation.reason: Polysemanticity is assumed to cause Knowledge Entanglement and motivates the SAE design. The overlap analysis is only an illustration, and the results evaluate the paper's own method.

tranche.reason: The paper uses neuron polysemanticity as motivation for an SAE-based editing method and mainly reports editing performance. Its only related analysis is a pairwise set overlap of activated neurons (Fig 1 e-f). That is a related but different construct, not a per-neuron polysemanticity measure, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: The figure-only overlap (up to 18%) is a set overlap of activated units for one unnamed model and layer, with unit type (MLP vs residual) unstated. There is no baseline for the overlap expected under dense activation, so it is illustrative and does not test any version.
